title: Finance companies cannot seize vehicles by force through recovery agents
summary: In Sadab Ahmad v. State of U.P. (Writ-C No. 36407 of 2026), a Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court held that a finance company cannot repossess a vehicle through recovery agents who use force, intimidation or firearms, even if the loan agreement allows repossession on default. The truck had been taken from the borrower, whose loan was with HDB Financial Services. The Court ordered the vehicle returned and awarded Rs 10,000 costs.
key_points: A repossession clause in a loan agreement does not allow force. A private financier cannot use the State's coercive power to enforce its own contract.
The Court did not decide whether the borrower had defaulted. That is for a civil court or the arbitrator.
It relied on Supreme Court rulings, including Magma Fincorp Ltd v. Rajesh Kumar Tiwari, that repossession cannot involve violence or intimidation.
The vehicle was ordered back to the borrower and the finance company was ordered to pay Rs 10,000 costs.
why_it_matters: Borrowers who fall behind on a vehicle loan still have rights. A lender must go to court or arbitration; it cannot send musclemen to take the vehicle.
source: Allahabad High Court (Justices J.J. Munir and Indrajeet Shukla); news report by LiveLaw Business, 13 Nov 2026

title: Gokul Dairy: no stay on ordinance giving State nominees a vote, but ballots kept separate
summary: The Kolhapur circuit bench of the Bombay High Court refused an interim stay on a Maharashtra ordinance that lets the State appoint nominated members with voting rights to large federal cooperative societies. The challenge was made in Shashikant Anandrao Patil v. Presiding Officer, Kolhapur Zila Sahakari Dudh Utpadak Sangh & Ors., over the Gokul Dairy polls. The Court directed that votes of elected directors and State nominees for choosing the chairperson be counted from separate ballots.
key_points: The High Court did not stop the ordinance for now. It refused an interim stay.
Elected directors and State-nominated directors must vote on separate ballots in the chairperson election.
The petition against the ordinance itself has not been finally decided.
why_it_matters: It shows how courts handle challenges to a government's power to put its own nominees on cooperative boards: they may allow the process to go on while keeping the nominees' votes separate until the case is decided.
source: Bombay High Court (Kolhapur circuit bench); news report by Bar & Bench, 10 Nov 2026

title: 60-day discharge window under BNSS applies to POCSO trials
summary: In Suvradip Halder v. State of West Bengal (CRR 307 of 2026), the Calcutta High Court (Justice Dr. Ajoy Kumar Mukherjee) held that the 60-day period in Section 250(1) of the BNSS for asking to be discharged also applies to POCSO trials. As the POCSO Act has no commitment procedure, the 60 days run from the day the accused is given the full set of prosecution documents. The Court set aside the order framing charges.
key_points: The accused in a POCSO trial gets the same 60-day window to seek discharge as other accused.
The 60 days start when the accused receives all the prosecution documents that will be relied on at trial.
The trial court must supply the missing documents within two weeks, and then decide any discharge application within 60 days.
The Court said the trial judge cannot act as a post office or mouthpiece of the prosecution, and linked fair process to Article 21.
why_it_matters: The new criminal procedure law gives accused persons a fixed time to seek discharge. This ruling makes clear that child-protection cases are not an exception, so fairness is not traded away for speed.
source: Calcutta High Court; news report by LiveLaw, 14 Nov 2026

title: Article 371A does not shield Naga customs that violate fundamental rights
summary: The Gauhati High Court (Justice Yarenjungla Longkumer) set aside orders excommunicating 38 petitioners and their families from a village in Nagaland after a dispute within a village union. The orders barred them from entering the village and from marrying villagers. The Court held that these orders violated Articles 14, 19 and 21 and quashed them.
key_points: A writ petition under Article 226 can lie against a private body that performs a public function or whose actions have a public-law element.
Article 371A protects Naga customary law, but customs are still subject to judicial review and cannot override fundamental rights (Article 13).
The excommunication also hit wives and children who had no part in the dispute.
The Court quashed the orders and announcements.
why_it_matters: Special constitutional protection for tribal customs does not put them above the Constitution. Individuals can still go to the High Court if a customary body takes away their basic rights.
source: Gauhati High Court; news report by LiveLaw, 13 Nov 2026

title: Drunk driving: licence can be suspended without waiting for a conviction
summary: Deciding a bail application in Geevarghese K.A. v. State of Kerala (B.A. No. 6173 of 2026), the Kerala High Court (Justice Kauser Edappagath) held that the Licensing Authority does not have to wait for criminal proceedings to end before using Section 19(1) of the Motor Vehicles Act to disqualify a person from holding a licence or to revoke it. The Court told the Transport Commissioner to make sure the power is used promptly in drunk-driving cases.
key_points: The Licensing Authority can reach its own view on the material before it. A conviction is not a precondition.
The Court noted that Section 19 powers are used only sparingly even as drunk-driving incidents rise.
Cases where an accident appears to be caused by intoxication should be examined without delay.
The accused was granted bail on conditions and his licence was sent to the Licensing Authority.
why_it_matters: A drunk-driving charge can now lead to loss of a licence long before the criminal trial ends.
source: Kerala High Court; news report by LiveLaw, 10 Nov 2026

title: Travel time to the magistrate is left out of the 24-hour limit on detention
summary: A Division Bench of the Telangana High Court (Justices Moushumi Bhattacharya and Renuka Yara) dismissed a habeas corpus petition in an NDPS case. It held that the time taken to travel from the police station to the Magistrate's court is excluded from the 24-hour limit, and that the 24 hours run from apprehension, not from the formal arrest. The two men had been held for 23 hours 45 minutes.
key_points: Article 22(2) of the Constitution and Section 58 of the BNSS require a person to be produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours.
Travel time to the Magistrate's court is not counted in those 24 hours.
The clock starts when a person is apprehended, not when the police record the formal arrest.
Habeas corpus is not the right route for disputed facts. The Court said other remedies against the remand order were open.
why_it_matters: Anyone who is detained must be brought before a Magistrate quickly. This ruling explains how the 24 hours are counted: from when liberty is actually restrained, and without the travel time.
source: Telangana High Court; news report by LiveLaw, 14 Nov 2026

title: Earning or married family members are not automatically barred from accident compensation
summary: In a motor accident appeal involving the deaths of a father and sister in 2015, the Delhi High Court (Justice Anish Dayal) held that a married, earning daughter, son, spouse or sibling cannot be excluded from compensation under the Motor Vehicles Act just because they are married, earn their own money or live separately. The Court increased the compensation for both deaths and awarded 9% interest.
key_points: Dependency is decided case by case, not by fixed categories of dependants and non-dependants.
All legal representatives can claim under Section 166 without proving dependency. Dependency affects the amount and how it is divided.
The claimant, who was married and lived separately, was treated as partly dependent on her parental family.
A wholly dependent claimant should receive a larger share than a partly dependent or independent one.
why_it_matters: A family member who earns or has moved out can still claim compensation after a fatal road accident.
source: Delhi High Court; news report by LiveLaw, 12 Nov 2026

title: Parents can claim compensation for the loss of an unborn child in a road accident
summary: The Punjab and Haryana High Court (Justice Parmod Goyal) held that parents can claim compensation under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 for the death of an unborn child in a road accident, and that a 28-week foetus is to be treated as a child for this purpose. The Court set aside a 2000 award of the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Panchkula, and allowed the appeal.
key_points: The Court followed the Kerala High Court Full Bench in Abhulasees P.P. v. Abdumanaf (2017).
It held that the Tribunal was wrong to rely on a Himachal Pradesh High Court ruling that such claims are not maintainable.
For the amount, the Court used the 1997 minimum wage for unskilled work, added 40% for future prospects and applied a multiplier of 9.
Compensation of Rs 2,27,072 with 7.5% interest was awarded.
why_it_matters: It recognises the loss that parents suffer when a pregnancy ends because of a road accident, and gives them a way to claim compensation.
source: Punjab and Haryana High Court; news report by LiveLaw, 10 Nov 2026

title: Admitting a relationship with a child's mother is not proof of paternity or grounds for a DNA test
summary: The Karnataka High Court (Justice Lalitha Kanneganti) held that a man's admission of a physical relationship with a child's mother is not conclusive proof of paternity and does not by itself justify a DNA test. It set aside a Family Court order directing a DNA examination and sent the application back for fresh consideration.
key_points: The Family Court must first look at other evidence, such as the circumstances of the relationship, the child's birth and any acknowledgment of parentage.
A DNA test is ordered only if that evidence is not enough. Any intrusion on privacy under Article 21 must be necessary and proportionate.
A child can claim maintenance whether or not the parents were married, but the father's liability must still be proved by evidence.
The child's welfare and need alone do not justify a DNA test.
why_it_matters: In paternity and maintenance disputes, a DNA test is not automatic. Courts weigh the privacy of the people involved and the strength of other evidence.
source: Karnataka High Court; news report by LiveLaw, 13 Nov 2026
